title: Choose the visual world
question: Choose how the first chess lesson should feel. Keep the assigned direction, take the alternate, use the familiar category layout, or ask for another hand.

options.label: Transit wayfinding
options.thesis: One clear route turns an unfamiliar board into a move the learner can read.
options.viewport: A familiar learning shell keeps the lesson and board legible; a single route traces b1 to c3.
options.risk: The transit metaphor could compete with the chessboard if routes spread beyond the move being taught.

raised.raise: A compact topic label keeps the learner oriented within the lesson.
Every piece keeps a consistent, unmistakable visual identity.
Keyboard focus and consequential actions remain clearly separated.
Color marks move states and feedback, never decoration alone.
Board coordinates and the move's origin and destination stay explicit.
Motion remains optional; reduced-motion keeps the lesson fully understandable.

options.label: Guided practice workbook
options.thesis: A worked example makes the first move feel learnable before the learner tries it.
options.viewport: The board is the exercise; a short example and one try-it prompt sit beside it.
options.risk: It may feel like a worksheet if examples and task states carry more weight than the live board.

options.label: Illustrated lexicon
options.thesis: Every chess idea appears as a categorized entry beside an illustrated plate.
options.viewport: A glossary entry explains the knight beside a diagram of its moves.
options.risk: A reference-book rhythm asks beginners to look things up instead of trying a move.
options.case: Less identifiable as an interactive first lesson and less direct about the learner's next action.
options.kept: Keep a concise lesson-range label so the learner knows where they are.

options.label: Character roster
options.thesis: Pieces become a roster of personalities with their own illustrated profiles.
options.viewport: The learner meets chess pieces as a ranked grid of characters.
options.risk: It assumes a playful, character-led audience and could distract from how the pieces move.
options.case: It has weaker audience fit without evidence that beginners want collectible characters, and weakens move clarity.
options.kept: Keep each chess piece's shape and identity consistent wherever it appears.

options.label: Dark developer console
options.thesis: A dense panel system turns the lesson into a technical analysis workspace.
options.viewport: Several persistent panels show the board, notation, and move metadata.
options.risk: A novice may read a technical tool as work they are not yet qualified to do.
options.case: The tool aesthetic is not grounded in a first-time learner's situation and adds technical signals without teaching value.
options.kept: Keep keyboard focus obvious and isolate controls that could reset learner work.

options.label: Guide-map landscape
options.thesis: A journey through a landscape represents the learner's progress through chess.
options.viewport: A large map shows the current lesson as one stop on a learning journey.
options.risk: The map takes space from the board and implies a larger curriculum that is not built yet.
options.case: A one-lesson MVP has no real journey to map, and the organic shape language fights the chess grid.
options.kept: Use color only where it identifies a move, a destination, or feedback state.

options.label: Star atlas
options.thesis: Coordinates and a traced path make the knight's destination feel discoverable.
options.viewport: A coordinate grid highlights the knight's start, destination, and possible moves.
options.risk: Constellation symbolism adds a second visual language to an already unfamiliar board.
options.case: Coordinates fit chess, but the star-chart world is not familiar enough to first-time learners and clouds the simple rule.
options.kept: Keep the board's coordinates and the start/end squares explicit.

options.label: Data field
options.thesis: High-contrast bars and a moving signal make each move feel like a live event.
options.viewport: The legal destinations pulse as a data pattern around the board.
options.risk: Strobing and abstract data are poor supports for a first lesson and can exclude some learners.
options.case: The world has little audience fit and the moving data obscures the concrete move the user must make.
options.kept: Respect reduced-motion preferences and keep the move readable in a static state.

canonCard.label: The familiar chess-learning app
canonCard.thesis: A clean lesson page places a standard chessboard beside an instruction panel.
canonCard.viewport: A conventional app header, lesson title, board, and move prompt make the task instantly familiar.
canonCard.risk: It is clear but deliberately less distinctive than the other directions.
